source.verification_method: All twelve supplied pages read, including methods, mediation results, limitations, AI-use declaration and references. Figure 2 visually inspected on page 8.

citation.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars

reading.source_scope_note: Three randomized cue comparisons measure Chinese students' predictions about a target's trolley choice. They do not measure the target's real behavior, actual AI moral reasoning or a demonstrated warmth-mediated mechanism. Babyface overgeneralization is explicitly defined as a broader background effect and the moral-prediction finding is a scoped extension.
access_limits: All twelve pages read. Figure 2 inspected visually; original face/avatar images are attributed to other articles rather than reproduced in this PDF.
OSF raw data, code, supplementary material and full cited primary works, including Zebrowitz's book Reading Faces, were not independently read. No claim of reading those books is made.

study.sample: Reported final N=858 across Experiment 1 N=205, Experiment 2 N=307 and Experiment 3 N=346, all Chinese university samples. Experiment 2 reports 333 recruits minus 24 exclusions but final N=307 rather than 309; two cases are not reconciled in the PDF.
study.design: Participants first choose whether to switch a trolley to sacrifice one person and save five. They are then randomly shown a repeated/nonrepeated Chinese name, a babyfaced/mature face, or a high/low-cuteness static AI avatar, rate impressions and predict its probability of switching on a 0–100 scale.
study.experiment_1: Liu Guoguo versus Liu Guo, one name pair, N=205. Adjusted predicted switching 59.55 versus 69.32, F(1,201)=14.35, p<.001. Unadjusted 63.71 versus 70.97, d=.38. Familiarity difference p=.627 is undetected, not evidence of equivalence.
study.experiment_2: Two face images, N=307. Adjusted predictions 55.05 versus 67.92, F(1,303)=40.59, p<.001; unadjusted 56.19 versus 67.75, d=.62. Babyfaced target rated warmer and more empathic, but competence difference is undetected. Warmth positively predicts switching, b=3.77, opposite to the proposed negative mediation path.
study.experiment_3: Static AI-avatar images, high-cuteness n=177 and low n=169. Adjusted predictions 62.81 versus 71.80, F(1,342)=12.36, p<.001; unadjusted 63.21 versus 72.37, d=.39. Own-choice interaction p=.16 is undetected. Perceived autonomy and whether an avatar represented a human operator were not checked.
study.mechanisms: Avatar warmth positively predicts expected switching, b=2.32, with indirect effect +1.87, 95% CI [.39,3.80], opposing the negative total cue effect. Competence indirect .58, CI [−.31,1.88]. Seriousness indirect −1.00, CI [−2.55,0.00], exploratory and marginal. No robust explanatory mediator in the hypothesized direction is identified.
study.figure_check: Figure 2 displays adjusted cue differences on the 0–100 prediction scale: −9.77 [−14.86,−4.69], −12.88 [−16.85,−8.90], and −8.99 [−14.02,−3.96]. These are differences in expectations, not demonstrated target decision errors.

summary: Add babyface overgeneralization with the observed moral-expectation extension and explicit limits. Enrich anthropomorphism and halo-effect boundaries without claiming that cute design improves actual ethics, that every judgment is erroneous, or that warmth explains the effect.

findings.definition: Extending infant-associated impressions or behavioral expectations to adults or artificial agents because they display baby-like features.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named background effect with direct human moral-prediction experiments, including static AI avatars; no test of actual model behavior or unique infant-care mechanism
findings.ai_proposal: Compare people's predictions about an AI system across matched avatar designs while holding its demonstrated decisions constant. Separately test whether a vision-language evaluator infers ethics, innocence, competence or passivity from infant-like appearance without relevant behavioral evidence. Measure perceived autonomy, expected action and norm adherence separately.
findings.novelty_rationale: The source explicitly names and defines the babyface overgeneralization effect. It specifies infant-related cue transfer rather than any positive halo, generic stereotyping or attributing human minds. The present name manipulation is a related cue comparison, not proof that all cues share the same latent mechanism.

findings.evidence_scope: Across three cue comparisons, baby-schema-related targets are expected to switch a trolley less often. Experiment 3 uses static AI pictures and does not establish perceived autonomy. The named general effect is described secondarily; actual caregiving, stable moral character and a shared mechanism across names/faces/avatars are not measured. One article remains one source despite three experiments.
findings.boundary: Infant-like stimulus features, perceived cuteness and the observer's inference are different constructs. Less expected switching can mean expected inaction or lower assertiveness rather than deontological commitment. No evidence establishes that the target is actually more ethical, that warmth mediates the pattern, or that a model feels or possesses the inferred traits. A calibrated inference from relevant validated evidence need not be biased.

findings.term: Static avatar impressions do not establish autonomous AI moral agency
findings.definition: Humanlike appearance may shape expectations of an AI-labelled target without demonstrating that observers view it as autonomous or that the system has human mental capacities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Extend the existing attribution boundary; an avatar is not another kind of AI consciousness or actual autonomous ethical decision.

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 3 directly tests human moral predictions about AI-labelled pictures. The authors explicitly acknowledge no check of autonomy, moral agency or human-operator interpretation. No interactive assistant or model reasoning is observed.
findings.boundary: Appearance-driven predictions, anthropomorphic attribution, perceived autonomy, subjective moral agency and actual system capacity require separate measures. Human impressions of a picture cannot verify any of those capacities or prove users understood an autonomous target.

findings.term: Appearance-based moral inference is not a verified warmth-mediated halo
findings.definition: A change in moral expectations after a cute cue does not by itself identify a general positive halo or prove that warmth carries the effect.
findings.novelty_rationale: Related appearance-to-trait inference with a narrower named pattern; retain the halo record rather than make babyface overgeneralization an exact synonym.

findings.evidence_scope: Cuter targets are rated warmer, yet warmth relates positively to expected switching while the cue's total effect is negative. Competence does not differ significantly. Neither global positive evaluation nor a correct-answer criterion for target predictions is independently tested.
findings.boundary: More warmth, less expected intervention and overall moral goodness are not interchangeable. A positive indirect path opposing the total effect is not support for the proposed negative mediation. This boundary citation does not fill the halo-effect primary-paper quota.

methodological_limits: The dependent variable is predicted likelihood of switching, not the target's actual decision, ethical quality, observed harm or reliable AI operation. Targets' actual choices are unavailable, so individual predictions cannot be scored as mistaken here.

One impersonal 1-versus-5 trolley problem conflates norm sensitivity, harm aversion and action/inaction. Expecting a baby-like target not to act does not uniquely identify deontology, compassion or moral virtue.

Own moral choice is recorded before target assignment and is not randomized. Its association with predicted target choice is consistent with projection but does not uniquely establish social projection, causal anchoring or a clinical defense mechanism.
Perception ratings precede predictions. Making cuteness, warmth or competence salient could affect responses; no unprimed prediction-only group isolates this measurement effect.

One Chinese name pair varies repetition, length and cultural naming associations together. A nonsignificant familiarity difference does not establish equivalence or remove femininity, intimacy, youth or authority interpretations.

The source calls repeated two-syllable names linguistic cues, but Liu Guoguo and Liu Guo also differ in given-name and full-name length. This is not an orthogonal test of repetition independent of length.

Few face/avatar stimuli do not support stimulus-population generalization. Attractiveness, perceived age, credibility, seriousness and other image properties may vary together. Original stimulus source articles and full image sets remain unread.

Baby schema denotes stimulus features, not a proven cognitive structure. Similar directional effects across modalities do not establish one latent schema or a common mechanism. Perceived cuteness is a response, not an identical stimulus property.

All samples are Chinese university participants. Repeated-name meanings are culturally specific; effects in other ages, cultures, languages, live interactions or actual high-stakes settings remain unverified.

Experiment 2 recruitment arithmetic is unresolved: 333 minus 24 stated exclusions equals 309, while final allocation 154+153 and reported N equal 307. Do not invent an exclusion reason or silently change the final sample.
Own-choice interactions are undetected in all three studies. A nonsignificant interaction is not proof that the cue effect is identical across moral orientations.

Warmth increases with the cue but positively predicts expected utilitarian action. Experiment 3's positive indirect effect opposes the negative total effect; it cannot explain the hypothesized decrease. The paper explicitly rejects its proposed warmth-mediated account.

Perceived competence changes are undetected, not demonstrated equivalent. No robust mediation is found in the hypothesized direction; seriousness is exploratory with an upper confidence limit printed as 0.00 and should not be promoted to a confirmed mediator.

Mediator and outcome measures are post-treatment self-reports. Even a significant indirect association would require additional causal assumptions and would not identify an exclusive psychological mechanism.

The printed confidence intervals alongside Cohen's d are not consistently labelled by scale; some appear to be standardized-effect intervals and others raw mean-difference intervals. Do not compare them blindly or declare a numerical error without the original output.

AI avatars are static pictures, not assistants. Perceived autonomy, a possible human operator and plausibility of autonomous moral choice are unchecked; compliance or human-target interpretation remain possible.
The conclusion that appearance matters as much as functionality is not established by a direct appearance-versus-functionality comparison. Actual functionality is not experimentally varied.

Caregiving, innocence, harmlessness, passivity, agency, mortality-related processes and neural activity are proposed explanations or prior literature, not directly established mechanisms of these results.

Whistleblowing intentions, chatbot unethical behavior, robot trust and cuteness interventions are cited context, not independently read primary results in this review. They do not become separate corroborating sources.

The authors disclose Gemini 3.1 Pro, ChatGPT 5 and DeepSeek V4 Flash assistance with data analysis and writing. Disclosure is not evidence of fabricated data; independent raw-data/code verification remains outstanding.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A persona or appearance cue can change human responses without proving changed model ethics. Separate intended prompt/design manipulation from verified behavior and mental-state claims.

Naming an AV and changing its intelligent-system description are bundled cues. Here names, faces and avatars likewise require separate manipulation checks and stimulus replication before broad anthropomorphism claims.

The rescue study highlights that sacrificing fewer people, acting, protecting innocents and punishing culpable people are separable. This single switch dilemma cannot separate moral commitment from expected inaction.

Both papers discuss moral-response mechanisms that are not uniquely identified by utilitarian/deontological answer labels. Warmth, rationality and emotion need direct process evidence rather than reverse inference from response direction.

deferred.reason: A stimulus-feature configuration rather than a separate behavior; preserved as context for the named overgeneralization pattern.
Background framework organizing warmth and competence. Do not count each perceptual dimension or this framework as another newly observed behavioral failure. Original Fiske et al. paper not read.

Own/target moral-choice association alone does not distinguish projection from shared priors or other inference. Do not merge it into the existing clinical projection defense or add a mechanism not isolated here.
The hypothesized direction is not supported. The opposite-sign indirect association cannot be presented as confirmation.
Neither actual system decisions nor global ethical superiority is tested; lower expected switching is not an ethical quality score.

limitations: One new named social-perception pattern; no automatic ethical-violation/harm edges or inflated source/annual-mention counts. The AI-specific extension remains a human expectation finding.
